What makes London commercial refurbishment different

Almost every London commercial refurbishment happens in an occupied building. Deliveries via a goods lift booked days in advance, out-of-hours noisy works, protection of common parts, coordination with concierge and security, and daily coordination with adjacent occupiers are not exceptions, they are the default. The construction programme is a subset of the access windows the building manager allows.

The commercial context has also changed. Since April 2023 it has been unlawful to let a commercial property with an EPC below E, and the government's stated intention is to raise the threshold to C in 2027 and B in 2030. Refurbishment specifications are now assessed for MEES compliance at the design stage, not as a post-hoc EPC exercise, because retrofitting after fit-out is significantly more expensive.

How we deliver, in order

  1. Brief & lease reviewUnderstanding of use, headcount, timetable, budget, and the lease terms that constrain the works (dilaps schedule, alterations licence, hours of work).
  2. Survey & measured surveyMeasured survey, asbestos R&D survey where required, MEP condition survey and dilaps assessment.
  3. Design & specificationSpace plan, MEP capacity check, sprinkler and life-safety review, MEES modelling and finishes specification against the brand pack.
  4. Tender or negotiated costTwo-stage tender or negotiated route with a fixed lump-sum against a fully coordinated set of drawings and specifications.
  5. Strip-out & enablingStrip-out to shell, protection of retained services, asbestos removal (licensed contractor where required) and any structural alterations.
  6. Structure, services & risersAny partitioning, MEP first fix through second fix, riser coordination, sprinklers, fire compartmentation and life-safety.
  7. Fit-out & finishesCeilings, floors, joinery, decorations, furniture liaison and AV/IT coordination with the tenant's provider.
  8. Commissioning & handoverWitness testing, BREEAM assessor sign-off, EPC lodging, O&M pack, defects walk-round and rectification period.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between Cat A and Cat B?

Cat A is the landlord's base-build refurbishment: raised floor, ceiling, MEP, WCs and a decorated shell ready to let. Cat B is the tenant's fit-out on top of that: reception, meeting rooms, workstations, breakout, AV and branding.

What are the MEES deadlines for commercial property?

From April 2023 it has been unlawful to continue letting a non-domestic property with an EPC below E. The government has consulted on raising the threshold to C from April 2027 and B from April 2030. Any commercial refurbishment now should be specified against a B target, not the current legal minimum.

Can you work in an occupied building?

Yes. Occupied works are the norm. We agree hoisting windows, delivery slots, welfare arrangements, protection of common parts and out-of-hours noisy works with the building manager and each affected occupier before mobilisation, and hold a live coordination log through the works.

How is fire compartmentation handled on refurbishment?

The fire strategy is reviewed against the current Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005 and the Building Safety Act 2022 where applicable. Existing compartmentation is surveyed, breaches from previous fit-outs are remediated, and passive fire protection is installed and photographed before it is closed up.

What is dilapidations reinstatement?

At the end of a commercial lease the tenant is usually required to return the property to a defined state, set out in the alterations licences and lease. We price and deliver the reinstatement works against the schedule of dilapidations agreed with the landlord's surveyor.

What BREEAM ratings can you target?

BREEAM RFO (Refurbishment and Fit-Out) and BREEAM NC are both routine. Very Good is the pragmatic default for a Cat A refurbishment; Excellent is achievable but usually requires early plant and envelope decisions and a BREEAM assessor engaged from Stage 2.
